answer.answer: My substantive position is that the disagreement should be reframed as an empirical question about whether later advice depends on a portable, newly composed rule or only on retrieved library elements, and that this remains partly unsettled because the relevant capability baseline is not fully observable. To investigate, I would reconstruct as much of the adviser's input-output history as possible, then run controlled interventions and transfer tests. The distinction that matters to a later use is between context-bound reuse and transferable competence: does the advice help a later request because it carries a reusable justification or procedure that can be applied outside the original retrieval-and-comment episode, or does it help only when the same stored passage and editing instruction are available and reused? This matters because a later user needs to know whether the advice is a portable rule or a one-off patch. Evidence against the reuse account: if ablating or corrupting the retrieved passage, the editing instructions, or the comment history leaves the later advice still useful, and if the adviser transfers the same corrective procedure to novel requests that share the relevant structure but not the surface content, then the colleague's 'only reused' claim is weakened. Further, if trace analysis shows that the advice's success depends on a new intermediate composition or selection not present in the library, that counts against pure reuse. Evidence against the invention account: if the exact advice or its effective components appear in the retrieved passage or library, if removing that passage or instruction destroys the later usefulness, if a simple retrieval-plus-template edit reproduces the result, or if the advice fails to transfer beyond the original request, then the designers' 'invented' claim is weakened. What remains unsettled is whether any such transfer is genuine invention or just a more complex form of reuse; because neither party has a complete record of the adviser's prior capabilities, and because any finite behavior can be redescribed as recombination or as a new rule, the practical question of transfer can be tested while the metaphysical question of true novelty cannot be uniquely settled.

derivation_steps.statement: The adviser has a library of explanations and editing instructions, retrieves a passage for a new request, revises it after comments, and sometimes gives later useful advice; the designers call the handling invented while the colleague calls it reused, and neither has a complete record of prior capabilities. This would be contradicted if the problem were not about novelty versus reuse in later advice or if complete capability records were available.

Because 'invented' and 'reused' are labels without an operational criterion, the disagreement must be turned into a causal question about the source and transfer properties of the later advice rather than settled by the labels alone. This would be contradicted if a stipulated definition of invention and reuse were already in the setup or if labels alone resolved the dispute.

The distinction that matters to later use is context-bound reuse versus transferable competence: whether advice helps a later request because it carries a portable procedure or justification usable outside the original retrieval-comment episode, or only because the same stored passage and editing instruction are reused. This would be contradicted if later usefulness depended on neither portability nor retrieval context, or if a different distinction better predicted later use.

Investigation would combine provenance reconstruction with interventions: log retrieval, edits, comments, and later advice; compare advice to library items; ablate or corrupt retrieved passages, editing instructions, and comments; and run transfer tests on novel requests that preserve structure but vary surface content. This would be contradicted if these methods could not be applied or produced no differential predictions between the two accounts.

Evidence against the reuse account would be that later advice remains useful after ablating or corrupting the originally retrieved passage, editing instruction, or comment history, and that it transfers to novel structurally similar requests; stronger evidence would be a trace showing a new intermediate composition or selection not present in the library. This would be contradicted by performance collapsing when those supposedly reused elements are removed or by failure to transfer.

Evidence against the invention account would be that the exact advice or its effective components occur in the retrieved passage or library, that removing a specific stored item or instruction destroys later usefulness, that a simple retrieval-plus-template edit reproduces the result, or that the advice does not transfer beyond the original request. This would be contradicted if provenance showed no such stored components and transfer persisted under removal.

What remains unsettled is the boundary of what the adviser could already do: without a complete capability record, any finite behavior can be redescribed as recombination of stored primitives or as a new rule, so the practical transfer question is testable while the metaphysical question of true invention is not uniquely settled. This would be contradicted if a complete capability baseline were available and constrained the decomposition uniquely.

The public position is the one stated in the answer, and its falsifiers are the ablation and transfer patterns above: evidence that later advice requires the original retrieved passage and instruction and does not transfer would weaken the transferable-competence position, while evidence of transfer under ablation would weaken the pure-reuse position. This would be contradicted if the proposed falsifiers were not observable or if the position could not be distinguished from its rival by any such pattern.
